Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Drawings
The drawings are objected to under 37 CFR 1.83(a).  The drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims.  Therefore, the “charging loop 1”, the “protecting loop 2” and the “communication control loop 3” must be shown/identified on Fig. 2 or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s).  No new matter should be entered.  Although each of these elements are illustrated in Fig. 1, there is no connection to how these three groups are tied to the elements illustrated in Fig. 2. Because of this it is difficult, if not impossible, to identify which components make up each of these three main groups as illustrated in Fig. 1.
Also, the drawings must show every feature of the invention specified in the claims.  Therefore, the “voltage detection unit” (see claim 8) must be shown or the feature(s) canceled from the claim(s).  No new matter should be entered.
Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Specification
The disclosure is objected to because of the following informalities: Although the term “own” is used 14 times in the specification, the term does not appear to carry the standard understanding of this term, thus making the application difficult to understand. In the interest of compact prosecution, the examiner will make a best guess of what is meant by the limitations in the claim language. The examiner suggests the applicant consider rewording the areas in the specification where “own” is used to provide a less ambiguous understanding of the claimed invention.
Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claims 1-10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the enablement requirement.  The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to enable one skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and/or use the invention.
It appears the inventor(s) filed the current application with a machine translation from a foreign language. While machine translations may be acceptable in some cases, there are cases when the machine translation does not accurately translate what was meant by the applicant.  In particular the use of the word “loop” appears to be incorrectly translated, and based on the application as a whole, the examiner believes the term may be used to mean “circuit” or “circuitry”, i.e. “charging circuitry”, “protecting circuitry” and “communication control circuitry”.
Likewise the term “an own” as used in claims 1 and 3, and “the own” as used in claim 2 appear to mean the charging parameter for a particular battery/battery-type as used in claims 1 and 2, and a detection program for a particular battery type?  It is not clear what the applicant is attempting to claim, but in the interest of compact prosecution, the examiner will make a best guess of what is meant by the limitations.
Note
For the purposes of this rejection, the term “loop” is understood to mean “circuit” or “circuitry”, and the term “an own” or “the own” is understood to mean for a particular element. Although the term “own” is used 14 times in the specification, the term does not appear to carry the standard understanding of this term, thus making the application difficult to understand. In the interest of compact prosecution, the examiner will make a best guess of what is meant by the limitations in the claim language.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1, 5 and 7-10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Xiong et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0052101 A1 (hereinafter Xiong) in view of Sussman et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0092183 A1 (hereinafter Sussman).
Regarding Claim 1, Xiong teaches an intelligent charging pile for a robot (Xiong, Fig. 1, Element 10; Para. [0008], Lines 1-2, “recharging dock”, and Title, “Robot Recharging Dock …”), comprising a charging loop (Xiong, Fig. 1, Element 12, and Fig. 2, Element 122; Para. [0012], “output circuit”, Para. [0013], Lines 4-7, and Paras. [0020] – [0022]), a protecting loop (Xiong, Fig. 2, Elements 121; Para. [0012], “switch controlling circuit”, and Paras. [0013] – [0019], Elements 121A&B), and a communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”), wherein, the charging loop is connected with the protecting loop, the protecting loop is connected with the communication control loop, and the communication control loop controls the charging loop to be turned off by means of controlling the protecting loop to be turned off (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]), but does not explicitly teach acquiring battery information of the robot and sending an adjustment instruction for charging the robot.
Sussman, however, teaches the communication control loop is connected with the charging loop (Sussman, Fig. 19; Paras. [0110] – [0117]), and the communication control loop is further used for acquiring battery information data of the robot (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 852, 858 and 860; Paras. [0134] – [0138]) and sending, according to the battery information data, an adjustment instruction to the charging loop, and the charging loop is used for adjusting, according to the adjustment instruction, an own charging parameter and charging, according to the adjusted charging parameter, the robot (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 862-874; Paras. [0139] – [0140], “using current selected from the particular charging profile being used”).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to understand that although Xiong is silent as to the details of acquiring battery information of the robot in order to adjust the charging as suggested in paragraph [0009], Xiong would inherently incorporate some type of conventional communication circuitry commonly understood in the art.  The communication circuitry taught by Sussman, for controlling the charging of the rechargeable battery, teaches one of the many conventional battery charging circuits utilized in the art for charging a battery.  A person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to choose based on desirability, one of the many known conventional methods, such as the one taught by Sussman, to control the charging of the battery of the robot within the robot recharging dock of Xiong.
Regarding Claim 5, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13, “sensing circuit”) is used for detecting whether the robot establishes a communication connection with the charging pile (Xiong, Paras. [0009] – [0011]).  Furthermore, Sussman teaches acquiring, after detecting that the robot establishes a communication connection with the charging pile, the battery information data sent by the robot (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 852, 858 and 860; Paras. [0134] – [0138]).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to understand that although Xiong is silent as to the details of acquiring battery information of the robot in order to adjust the charging as suggested in paragraph [0009], Xiong would inherently incorporate some type of conventional communication circuitry commonly understood in the art.  The communication circuitry taught by Sussman, for controlling the charging of the rechargeable battery, teaches one of the many conventional battery charging circuits utilized in the art for charging a battery.  A person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to choose based on desirability, one of the many known conventional methods, such as the one taught by Sussman, to control the charging of the battery of the robot within the robot recharging dock of Xiong.
Regarding Claim 7, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”) further comprises a charging control unit, and the charging control unit is used for making a logic determination on the battery information data and sending, after the logic determination shows no error, the adjustment instruction to the charging loop (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]).
Regarding Claim 8, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”) further comprises a voltage detection unit, and the voltage detection unit is connected with the robot and is used for detecting a charging voltage of the robot, the charging control unit is further used for controlling, when the voltage detection unit detects that the charging voltage is not within a preset voltage range, the protecting loop to be turned off, so as to cause the charging loop to stop charging the robot (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]).
Regarding Claim 9, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Sussman teaches wherein the communication control loop further comprises a display unit, and the display unit is in communication connection with the robot and is used for displaying a state of charge of the robot (Sussman, Fig. 13A, Element 526; Paras. [0089] and [0115]).
Absent of showing criticality of the displaying battery information of Xiong, it would have been an obvious matter of design choice to use the display of Sussman based on desirability, since applicant has not disclosed that this type of display solves any stated problem or is for any particular purpose and it appears that the invention would perform equally well with other types of battery state status.
Regarding Claim 10, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Sussman teaches wherein the battery information data comprises at least one of a battery type, a battery parameter, and a state of health of the battery (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 852, 858 and 860; Paras. [0134] – [0138]).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to understand that although Xiong is silent as to the details of acquiring battery information of the robot, Xiong would inherently incorporate some type of conventional communication circuitry commonly understood in the art.  The communication circuitry taught by Sussman, for controlling the charging of the rechargeable battery, teaches one of the many conventional battery charging circuits utilized in the art for charging a battery.  A person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to choose based on desirability, one of the many known conventional methods, such as the one taught by Sussman, to control the charging of the battery of the robot within the robot recharging dock of Xiong.
Claims 2-4 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Xiong et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0052101 A1 (hereinafter Xiong) in view of Sussman et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0092183 A1 (hereinafter Sussman) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Koyanagi et al. U.S. PGPub 2006/0043929 A1 (hereinafter Koyanagi).
Regarding Claim 2, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein the charging loop (Xiong, Fig. 1, Element 12, and Fig. 2, Element 122; Para. [0012], “output circuit”, Para. [0013], Lines 4-7, and Paras. [0020] – [0022]) comprises a power supply input socket (Xiong, Fig. 2, Element 14).
Furthermore, Sussman teaches the charging module is connected with the communication control loop (Sussman, Fig. 19; Paras. [0110] – [0117]) and is used for adjusting, according to the adjustment instruction, the own charging parameter (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 862-874; Paras. [0139] – [0140], “using current selected from the particular charging profile being used”), and the contactable electrode is connected with the robot and is used for charging, according to the adjusted charging parameter, the robot (Sussman, Fig. 19, Element 200; Para. [0110]).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to understand that although Xiong is silent as to the details of acquiring battery information of the robot in order to adjust the charging as suggested in paragraph [0009], Xiong would inherently incorporate some type of conventional communication circuitry commonly understood in the art.  The communication circuitry taught by Sussman, for controlling the charging of the rechargeable battery, teaches one of the many conventional battery charging circuits utilized in the art for charging a battery.  A person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to choose based on desirability, one of the many known conventional methods, such as the one taught by Sussman, to control the charging of the battery of the robot within the robot recharging dock of Xiong.
The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above, but does not explicitly teach the details of the power supply input, charging module and contactable electrode(s)
Koyanagi, however, teaches wherein the charging loop (Koyanagi, Fig. 4, Element 60; Para. [0039]) comprises a power supply input socket (Koyanagi, Fig. 4, Element 70; Para. [0042]), a charging module (Koyanagi, Fig. 4, Elements 61-64; Para. [0042]), and a contactable electrode (Koyanagi, Fig. 4, Elements 30; Para. [0043]), wherein, the power supply input socket is connected with a mains supply and is used for introducing an input power supply (Koyanagi, Para. [0042]), the charging module is connected with the communication control loop (Koyanagi, Fig. 4, Element 50; Para. [0039]).
Absent of showing criticality of the elements making up the power module of the charging device of Xiong, it would have been an obvious matter of design choice to use the power module layout of Koyanagi based on desirability, since applicant has not disclosed that this type of power module solves any stated problem or is for any particular purpose and it appears that the invention would perform equally well with other types of power module layouts.
Regarding Claim 3, The combined teaching of the Xiong, Sussman and Koyanagi references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claims 2/1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein a sensor (Xiong, Fig. 2, Element 131; Paras. [0010] – [0011]) is arranged in the contactable electrode (Xiong, Fig. 1, Element 11; Para. [0008]), and the sensor is used for detecting whether contact between the charging pile and the robot meets a preset requirement (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]), and the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”) is connected with the sensor and is used for enabling, when the sensor detects that the contact between the charging pile and the robot meets the preset requirement, an own detection program (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]).
Regarding Claim 4, The combined teaching of the Xiong, Sussman and Koyanagi references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claims 3/2/1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches wherein the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”) comprises an alignment detection unit, the alignment detection unit is connected with the contactable electrode, and the alignment detection unit is used for detecting, when the sensor detects that the contact between the charging pile and the robot meets the preset requirement, whether the robot has been aligned with the charging pile, and the communication control loop is used for controlling, after it is detected that the robot has been aligned with the charging pile, the protecting loop to be turned on, so as to enable the contactable electrode to charge the robot (Xiong, Fig. 2; Para. [0009]).
Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Xiong et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0052101 A1 (hereinafter Xiong) in view of Sussman et al. U.S. PGPub 2019/0092183 A1 (hereinafter Sussman) as applied to claim 1 above, and further in view of Yamada et al. U.S. PGPub 2013/0308239 A1 (hereinafter Yamada).
Regarding Claim 6, The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above in claim 1.  Furthermore, Xiong teaches the communication control loop (Xiong, Figs. 1-2, Element 13; Paras. [0009] – [0011], “sensing circuit”).  Furthermore, Sussman teaches a manual control unit (Sussman, Fig. 22, step 854; Para. [0138]) and a storage unit, and the storage unit stores the battery information data of various kinds of robots, and the manual control unit is used for detecting whether the battery information data in the storage unit is called and taking, when detecting that the battery information data in the storage unit is called, the called battery information data as the battery information data of the robot (Sussman, Fig. 22, steps 852, 858 and 860; Paras. [0134] – [0138]).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to understand that although Xiong is silent as to the details of acquiring battery information of the robot in order to adjust the charging as suggested in paragraph [0009], Xiong would inherently incorporate some type of conventional communication circuitry commonly understood in the art.  The communication circuitry taught by Sussman, for controlling the charging of the rechargeable battery, teaches one of the many conventional battery charging circuits utilized in the art for charging a battery.  A person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to choose based on desirability, one of the many known conventional methods, such as the one taught by Sussman, to control the charging of the battery of the robot within the robot recharging dock of Xiong.
The combined teaching of the Xiong and Sussman references discloses the claimed invention as stated above, but does not teach a storage unit, although it is implied by the disclosure.
Yamada, however, teaches wherein the communication control loop comprises a manual control unit and a storage unit, and the storage unit stores the battery information data (Yamada, Fig. 1, Element 15; Para. [0050]).
Absent of showing criticality of the storage unit to hold battery information for the battery of the robot of Xiong, it would have been an obvious matter of design choice to use the memory storage of Yamada based on desirability, since applicant has not disclosed that this type of storage solves any stated problem or is for any particular purpose and it appears that the invention would perform equally well with other types of data storage methods.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure.
Wu U.S. PGPub 2002/0109485 teaches a battery charging device configured for different battery types along with protection devices.
Caussy et al. U.S. PGPub 2020/0249688 teaches a robot docking station retrieving battery information from the robot.
